rulings.title: How to say dhamma
rulings.statement: One Indic word, dhamma, does three jobs in Pairs. In verses 1–2 the plural dhammā means what the mind goes before: our states of mind and what we experience. In verse 20 it is the Buddha's teaching. (Verse 5 is ruled separately in R-T2-02.) The Chinese 法/道 and Tibetan ཆོས translate the same word, so they agree; the Chinese 道 'the Way' is not a separate reading. Both readers advise against 'experience', the current placeholder's word, as adding an interpretation.

options.text: Verses 1–2: “things”. Literal, close to the Chinese 法 'all things' and the Tibetan 'phenomena', and leaves the meaning open.
Verses 1–2: “states” or “mental states”. Narrower and clearer about what is meant, but “mental” is ours.
Verse 20, the teaching: “the teaching” in plain words, not “the Dhamma” untranslated.

rulings.title: “This is an age-old principle”, not “eternal law” (verse 5)
rulings.statement: Verse 5 ends esa dhammo sanantano. Sanantano means 'from of old, perpetual'. “Eternal” asserts eternity, a metaphysical claim; “age-old” says only that it is ancient. Neither the Tibetan ('the nature of things') nor the Chinese ('this way is worth honouring') says eternal. Both readers recommend “age-old”.

rulings.title: vera: “enmity”, not “hatred” (verses 3–5)
rulings.statement: Vera is enmity between people, a grudge held against someone; the Chinese 怨 'resentment' and the Tibetan 'grudge' agree. “Hatred” is better kept for dosa, the inner poison, which appears elsewhere. The placeholder says “hostility”.

rulings.title: Keep the pun on the stained robe (verses 9–10)
rulings.statement: The Pāli plays on kasāva 'stain, impurity' and kāsāva 'the ochre robe' (literally the dyed one): someone still stained wears the stained robe. The Chinese and Tibetan lose the pun. Literal+ allows a departure where the original has a beauty a plain rendering loses.

options.text: Keep it: “still stained… the stained ⟨ochre⟩ robe”.
Plain: “not free of impurities… the ochre robe”.

rulings.title: A glossary for recurring words
rulings.statement: Words that every tradition agrees on but that have several possible English renderings. Fixing them once keeps the whole book consistent. Approve the list as a block, or name the terms you want changed.

options.text: paduṭṭha / pasanna, the state of mind (1–2)
subha / asubha, as an object of attention (7–8)

rulings.title: Same idea, different word: follow the widest support
rulings.statement: Often the traditions say the same thing with a different word (Pāli 'never leaving' vs 'following' for the shadow in verse 2). Default: use the word with the widest support across independent traditions; on a tie, keep the Pāli word. In Pairs this changes only verse 2: “like a shadow that follows”.

options.text: Widest support; Pāli on a tie.

rulings.title: Count traditions by family, not by column
rulings.statement: The Tibetan translates the Sanskrit Udānavarga, so the two count as one voice. Where the Tibetan alone departs from its Sanskrit, it is a Tibetan translation matter and is not followed. Example: in verse 1 the Tibetan has “like a head cut off by a wheel” where everyone else has the wheel following the ox.

options.text: Count the Tibetan as its own voice.

rulings.title: A lone voice gives way
rulings.statement: A reading found in only one tradition gives way to a different reading shared by two or more others. It is recorded, not followed. A fragment of a damaged manuscript can confirm a reading but never carry one alone. Example: the Gāndhārī alone says “unguarded” where all others say “undeveloped” (verses 13–14).

options.text: Adopt, but exempt the Gāndhārī as the oldest manuscript, so its lone readings come to you.

rulings.title: The Chinese counts where it agrees, informs where it recasts
rulings.statement: The Chinese translator wrote in his own idiom. Where his words carry the same sense, that counts as agreement. Where he changes an image or a line (grass for a weak tree in verse 7; a herd of cattle in verse 19), it shows how an early reader understood the verse but does not replace what the Indic texts agree on.

options.text: Treat changed Chinese images as full variants.

rulings.title: Partial parallels and missing lines inform, not supply
rulings.statement: A partial parallel (a different verse that shares some lines) can confirm a reading but never adds or removes a line. The Blend keeps every Pāli line; where other traditions lack a line, that is noted, not treated as evidence against it.

options.text: Adopt: keep every line, line for line.
Drop or bracket lines most traditions lack.

rulings.title: When Pāli and Patna stand against Gāndhārī, Sanskrit and Tibetan
rulings.statement: Pāli and Patna are close relatives, and so are the Gāndhārī and the Udānavarga (Sanskrit and Tibetan). When the two groups disagree on a word that changes the meaning, the evidence is roughly even. Pairs has four such places (verses 3–4, 7–8, 9–10 and 19–20), listed below as T4 questions. Both readers advise deciding these one by one for now and revisiting once we see how often the pattern recurs.

options.text: Decide each one yourself (they come to you as T4s); revisit after Pairs.
Follow the Gāndhārī–Udānavarga side, as more independent witnesses.
